summary: At 25 people per square mile spread across 3,510 square miles, Mendocino County is larger than Rhode Island and Delaware combined yet holds fewer residents than a single San Francisco neighborhood — a fact that defines nearly every tradeoff of living here. The landscape ranges from the dramatic sea stacks and coastal bluffs along Highway 1 to the inland valleys of Ukiah and Willits tucked between the Coast Ranges, where redwood forests give way to oak-studded hillsides and vineyards. That geography means stunning evening light over Pacific headwaters but also genuine isolation: healthcare, timber, agriculture, cannabis cultivation, and public-sector jobs anchor the economy, and switching employers without a long drive is a narrow proposition. A median home price of $486,000 against a median household income of roughly $64,700 produces a price-to-income ratio above 7.5 — expensive by rural standards, yet median rent at $1,325 remains accessible compared to the Bay Area that sits three hours south. Daily highs average a mild 66°F with nearly nine hours of sunshine, though coastal fog and inland heat create two distinct climates within a single county. The poverty rate of 15.2% and limited broadband infrastructure in outlying areas underscore a persistent tension: Mendocino delivers a landscape that rivals anywhere on the West Coast, paired with the economic fragility that extreme remoteness tends to produce.
